entry.content:
Challenges in Multilingual models

Uncertainty, Confidence and Calibration

In the context of multilingual language models, understanding and quantifying uncertainty is crucial for building reliable AI systems. Confidence estimation allows us to gauge how much trust we can place in a model’s predictions, while calibration ensures that these confidence scores accurately reflect the true likelihood of correctness. Techniques such as conformal prediction provide a principled framework for generating reliable confidence measures, enabling more robust and interpretable model outputs across diverse languages and tasks.

Conformal prediction is a statistical framework that provides confidence measures for model predictions by constructing prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the true outcome with a user-specified probability, under minimal assumptions. This approach enables models to quantify uncertainty in their outputs, making them more reliable and interpretable, especially in multilingual settings where data distribution may vary.

entry.title: Confidence Estimation for LLMs
entry.content:
While using large language models for various functionalities, we are often reminded that the model is not 100% reliable and can make mistakes. We need principled ways to decide when to trust a model’s output and when to dig deeper, especially for high-stakes settings such as medical and financial domains. I’ve always been fascinated by this issue. In this article, I will give an overview of how ideas from classical machine learning calibration and recent LLM research all fit together.

Uncertainty, Confidence and Calibration

Calibration and uncertainty estimation of predictions from ML models have a long history. These concepts are particularly important in computer vision and image classification, likely because many image classification applications involve high-stakes usage, such as medical image diagnosis.

  • Uncertainty reflects how spread-out a model’s predictive distribution is. We generally use entropy as a way to measure uncertainty, where a higher entropy means higher uncertainty.

  • Confidence Score for a prediction can be measured by its normalized probability under the model parameter \(\theta\). For example, we can say that a model with parameter \(\theta\) is \(90\%\) confident about the prediction \(y\) if $P(y|\theta) = 0.9$.

  • Calibration measures how correct the model’s self confidence is. People usually look at the calibration error rate, where a low error rate means the model is more calibrated. For example, among the examples where the model is 90% confident, the calibration error is 0 if they are indeed 90% correct, while the calibration error is larger if the actual accuracy deviates from 90%. It is worth noting that a lower calibration error doesn’t necessarily mean the model is more accurate. A perfectly calibrated model can still be inaccurate overall, while a highly accurate model can be poorly calibrated if it is sometimes over-confident. Recent studies show that LLMs might become less calibrated while having a higher accuracy rate after RLHF, usually because they become over-confident in the predictions .

How to Elicit Confidence from an LLM

Model calibration and confidence estimation has some new challenges in the age of LLMs. This is because standard autoregressive LLMs reformulate classification tasks into language generation tasks, providing a unified paradigm for any use cases. This paradigm allows us to provide a single unified model for both generation and classification, but it also creates new challenges of extracting model confidence from the prediction model. Next, we will introduce several popular methods for extracting confidence scores from LLMs.

1. Normalized class label probability

While it is less intuitive to get class probabilistic scores from labels generated from LLMs, we can still construct a similar confidence measure from the generative model as the traditional classification models. The major difference is that we need to manually normalize the probability scores across all possible class labels. For example, suppose we want to tackle a binary classification problem by prompting LLMs, we can set our class label space to be ${\text{yes}, \text{no}}$. For each example $x$, we need to call LLMs twice to get likelihood for each label $M(\text{yes}|x)$ and $M(\text{no}|x)$, and we can simply formulate the likelihood for positive label as

\[P(\text{yes}|x) = \frac{M(\text{yes}|x)}{M(\text{yes}|x) + M(\text{no}|x)}\]

2. Verbalized confidence score

Recent works found that LLMs are capable of generating the confidence score directly . This is a much more convenient way of getting confidence estimates from LLMs since it only requires prompt engineering and processing model generated text. It also allows us to get both the class label and confidence estimate in one LLM call, thus saving compute. While research found that this method is surprisingly reliable for very large models, it is less reliable for smaller or less capable models. It is also unclear how different post-training strategies, advances in RL and test-time training affect the reliability of verbalized confidence scores.

3. Confidence score by multiple choice

To alleviate the concerns for verbalized confidence score, researchers have proposed another prompt engineering trick to elicit confidence estimates from LLMs. Generally, the model could be more accurate at selecting from several well-defined options, than coming up with a score directly. Therefore, we could design confidence estimation into a multiple choice question, where each option represents a different level of confidence.

4. Self-consistency score

Another popular and more intuitive method to get confidence measures from LLMs is through self-consistency sampling . We can sample the class labels from LLMs multiple times, and usually choose the most frequent label as the final prediction. Consider a binary classification problem where the label space is ${\text{yes}, \text{no}}$, we can sample from the LLM $N$ times, where each time the model outputs either of the two labels. This setup allows us to define the LLM likelihood of this prediction as the percentage of times that the model outputs the given label, where a higher likelihood indicates higher confidence in the prediction. For example, the likelihood or confidence for the label to be yes can be formulated as

\[P(\text{yes}|x) = \frac{\#\{M(y|x) = \text{yes}\}}{N}\]

Potential Applications

Cost-effective Synthetic Data Curation

Synthetic data has become an important ingredient for LLM development. While it is very cost-effective to generate either synthetic pretraining data or model-based preference labels, a major factor for curating effective synthetic data is to ensure their quality. A common strategy is to combine synthetic generation with human review or revision, and this is where confidence estimation of LLM prediction can help. Instead of having humans reviewing all synthetic generations, we can significantly reduce the annotation cost by only asking human annotations on examples where LLM prediction has a low confidence score.

Similar strategies can be applied for model evaluation, where we need to collect human evaluation results. Researchers have proposed to use LLM to evaluate the model output and output a confidence score for the evaluation result . Given a human annotation budget, we can gather human evaluation results on the subset of examples where the model confidence score is low.

Adaptive Test-time Compute

Apart from saving human annotation cost, LLM confidence score can also save the inference cost of scaling test-time compute, especially for reasoning models. We can improve the capability of LLMs through inference-time compute, by generating multiple parallel samples for a single prompt, and combine the results for a final answer.

However, we know that not all questions are equally difficult. Some very hard questions might benefit more from test-time computation, while easier ones might not need additional test-time compute at all. Therefore, LLM confidence estimates could be used as the signal to determine which examples might require additional inference compute , which allows us to achieve a balance between prediction accuracy and computational cost. Specifically, we can use the self-consistency based uncertainty measure to keep sampling new responses from the LLM until the model is confident enough about the final conclusion.

Conformal Factuality Guarantee

Another interesting use case for LLM confidence scores is to post-process the output from an LLM such that we can have high confidence about the factuality or correctness of the output. Recent work proposed a framework that provides statistically valid guarantees on long-form generation from LLMs .

Conformal prediction is a statistics technique designed for classification tasks. For each input to be classified, it outputs a set of labels such that we are guaranteed to have the correct label in this set with high confidence. But how can we establish a similar statistical guarantee for the long-form output from an LLM? We probably want to still return a single paragraph output for a user query, so it is not practical to construct a set of LLM outputs and ask the users to identify which ones they should trust.

In this paper , researchers proposed an algorithm that allows us to post-process a long-form response from LLM where we can have a statistical guarantee for its correctness. Let $y$ be the original output from the LLM, the procedure operates in three general steps:

  1. we extract a set of atomic factual claims from the original response $y$ (using a call from LLM);
  2. for each claim, we can get a LLM-based confidence score indicating whether it is factually correct. There are few options for this step, and the authors experimented with both verbalized confidence and self-consistency scores;
  3. filter out the claims with confidence score below a certain threshold, and reconstruct the rest of the atomic claims into a final response.

This is a rather computationally expensive process, but it is an interesting idea for addressing the hallucination issues with LLMs.

Future Work

In this article, we introduce several methods to elicit confidence scores for LLM-based classifiers, and show that it can be a powerful tool for building new models or getting better predictions from existing models. Uncertainty scores for classification models have a simple and intuitive formulation, but it is less clear what is the best strategy for obtaining confidence scores from LLMs. We need a more systematic understanding of the trade-offs and interactions between different methods, such as verbalized confidence scores and self-consistency sampling. As new model behaviors emerge, it is also important to re-examine the conclusions we had about the earlier models.
